items.article_context_original: Concerns over the Treasury Department's debt repurchase program continue to weigh on markets. Longer-dated U.S. government bond yields moved higher on Friday as investor jitters over the Treasury Department's extended debt repurchase program and soaring national debt continued to hover over markets. The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond, one of the targets of the buyback plan, rose more than 3 basis points to 5.273%. A week ago, the long bond yielded 5.21%. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was up more than 3 basis points at 4.734%. Last Friday, the 10-year yielded as little as 4.63%. The shorter-dated 2-year Treasury note yield, which more closely tracks short-term Federal Reserve rate expectations, was higher by more than 4 basis points at 4.232%. A week, the two-year low yield was about 4.10%. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.

items.article_context_original: Science & Technology | Washington (TIP): The US Treasury Department said on Wednesday that it will more than double the size of its government debt buybacks. The move comes as Washington (TIP): The US Treasury Department said on Wednesday that it will more than double the size of its government debt buybacks. The move comes as the bond market is facing heavy pressure and Treasury yields have climbed to levels not seen in nearly 20 years. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is leading the department as it increases its role as a buyer in the government bond market, CNBC reported. The main aim is to support liquidity in the longer-term part of the Treasury market, where trading conditions have become difficult. Buybacks will target longer-term Treasury debt Under the new plan, Treasury will focus on government debt with maturities of 10 to 20 years and 20 to 30 years. These longer-term bonds have faced a buyers’ strike since late June, meaning investors have been less willing to buy them. The Treasury currently allows a maximum of $2 billion in each buyback operation. That amount will now be increased to at least $4 billion, meaning the size of the operations will at least double, according to the Treasury Department. The new plan will begin on September 9 and remain in place through November 4. Bond yields dropped after announcement Treasury’s announcement immediately pushed bond yields sharply lower, while US stock market futures moved higher. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield fell 6 basis points to 4.647%. The 30-year Treasury yield dropped 9 basis points to 5.196%. One basis point is equal to 0.01 percentage point. Treasury bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, so falling yields mean bond prices are rising. Why is the Treasury doing this? Treasury said the larger buyback operations are meant to provide more liquidity in longer-dated parts of the government bond market. The department said there is still strong interest from market participants in these longer-term bonds. items.article_context_original: Dollar slips as Treasury buybacks push long yields down; Fed stays cautious ahead of Jackson Hole risks. The US dollar slid over the past week as attention shifted from geopolitics and Fed expectations to the US bond market. After Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said the Treasury would buy back larger amounts of older, less-liquid long-dated government bonds, the dollar broke below 99.00 and later moved towards 98.50 for the first time since mid-May. The plan targets ‘off-the-run’ Treasuries to bolster liquidity and manage the debt profile, rather than QE, and the initial market response saw demand for longer-dated bonds rise while yields fell, weighing on the currency. The move also resurfaced fiscal concerns, with the dollar’s reaction running through lower long-term yields and shifting risk premia, including the potential for a bear steepener if long-end yields rise on fiscal or inflation fears. Fed messaging stayed cautious: Alberto Musalem put underlying inflation at 2.5% to 3%, above the 2% goal, while the July 28–29 FOMC minutes showed most backed no change though several preferred a rise, and fed staff described the outlook as slightly weaker. CFTC data for the week to 11 August showed net speculative dollar positioning down nearly 1.1K to about 21.4K contracts, with the four-week change at +8,230 versus +9,230, and open interest near 49.5K; exposure was 43.21%, with percentiles at 66.6 and 73.9. Next week brings Jackson Hole, plus revisions to Nonfarm Payrolls, another Q2 GDP reading and PCE inflation, while the dollar’s longer-run role remains tied to the Fed’s 2% target and its policy toolkit from QE to QT; the currency still dominates over 88% of global FX turnover, equal to $6.6 trillion a day in 2022. We suggest derivative traders closely watch the $30 trillion US Treasury market as the Treasury’s new buyback program reshapes the US Dollar’s trajectory. With the Greenback slipping below the 99.00 support level toward 98.50, we believe short-term pressure on the currency will persist. This liquidity-boosting initiative has successfully pushed long-term yields down, temporarily eroding the interest rate advantage that previously supported the Dollar

items.article_context_original: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has initiated a public comment period on a proposal by CBOE BZX Exchange to list the first leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs) in The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has initiated a public comment period on a proposal by CBOE BZX Exchange to list the first leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs) in the United States tied to three times the daily returns of Bitcoin and Ethereum. The filing, published by the regulatory body, marks a significant step in the ongoing integration of digital assets into mainstream financial products. CBOE BZX, the equities exchange arm of the Chicago Board Options Exchange, submitted a rule change proposal to list six leveraged ETFs. These include a 3x Bitcoin ETF, a 3x Ethereum ETF, and leveraged funds for gold, silver, crude oil, and natural gas. The leveraged structure aims to deliver daily returns that are three times the performance of the underlying asset, offering traders amplified exposure to price movements. The SEC’s decision to open the proposal for public comment is a procedural requirement under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. It allows interested parties—including investors, industry professionals, and academics—to submit feedback on whether the products meet the exchange’s listing standards and investor protection requirements. If approved, these would be the first leveraged crypto ETFs available on U.S. exchanges. While leveraged ETFs are common in traditional finance, their introduction to the crypto space could significantly alter how retail and institutional investors access digital assets. These products offer a way to gain magnified exposure without directly holding the underlying cryptocurrency, potentially increasing market liquidity and participation. However, leveraged ETFs carry heightened risk due to daily rebalancing and compounding effects, which can lead to unexpected losses over extended periods. The SEC’s scrutiny is expected to focus on these risks, as well as on the underlying market’s volatility and the ability of the fund sponsor to manage such products effectively.
